title: Realtime speech-to-speech
summary: A realtime speech-to-speech model hears audio, reasons, calls tools and speaks back inside one persistent session. You choose the transport, manage keys and sessions, and pay for audio tokens that grow with the conversation.
useIf: A person talks to the system live and low latency matters more than inspecting text between stages.
avoidIf: You must filter, log or rewrite the text before the model sees it, or the audio is recorded and nobody waits.

explain.md: In the **Realtime API** one speech-to-speech model runs per session. It interprets audio, decides what to do, calls tools and answers in speech over a persistent connection, which avoids chaining three services [[r3]]. OpenAI's docs also describe **GPT-Live**, a full-duplex model that listens while it speaks and delegates reasoning to a separate backend, and say to start new conversational voice apps there (checked 2026-10-13). This topic covers the Realtime API itself.

Inside a session you configure instructions, voice, tools and turn detection, then exchange JSON events: audio in, audio out and tool calls in between. No separate text stage sits between hearing and speaking, which removes a hop, but you also cannot gate the text before the model reasons. Keep instructions stable across the session, because mid-session edits break the prompt cache [[r5]].

rows: OpenAI mints ephemeral keys with `POST /v1/realtime/client_secrets`. GA calls use `/v1/realtime/calls` [[r3]]
On Azure use the GA `/openai/v1` endpoint and send no `api-version` [[r6]]
A client integration must terminate the audio, since Azure's API does not connect straight to end-user devices [[r6]]

explain.title: Browser session with an ephemeral key
explain.alt: The browser asks the app server for a key. The server mints an ephemeral key. The browser then opens a WebRTC session directly with the Realtime API.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant S as App server
  participant R as Realtime API
  B->>S: Request session
  S->>R: Mint ephemeral key
  R-->>S: Short-lived key
  S-->>B: Key
  B->>R: Open WebRTC session
  R-->>B: Audio and events

explain.title: Audio token accounting

vars.v: 1 token per 100 ms of user audio, 1 per 50 ms of assistant audio

explain.example: A turn of 8 s user audio and 16 s assistant audio is 80 + 320 = **400** tokens. The full conversation is resent each turn, so by turn 10 about 9 x 400 = 3,600 tokens of history precede the new audio (an estimate that assumes history stays audio). Prompt caching is best effort, and changing history or instructions mid-session busts the cache [[r5]].

explain.title: Beta to GA changes
explain.md: Drop the `OpenAI-Beta: realtime=v1` header, mint keys at `/v1/realtime/client_secrets`, use `/v1/realtime/calls`, set `session.type`, and use renamed events such as `response.output_audio.delta` [[r3]]. Azure sessions last at most 60 minutes [[r6]].

whereToUse: Browser voice assistants and tutors that talk back in real time
Server pipelines that bridge phone audio to a model
Hands-free assistants in vehicles or on devices
Voice front ends where interruptions and natural pauses matter

use: Latency and natural turn-taking are the top priority
One model can handle understanding, tools and speech
You accept less visibility into text between stages
avoid: Policy needs redaction or logging of text before the model reasons
A tuned text agent already exists and must stay in charge of logic
Sessions routinely exceed one hour with no reconnect design
flips: Browser client: WebRTC with ephemeral keys. Server bridge or telephony: WebSocket or SIP
Slow backend work must not freeze the call: consider GPT-Live style delegation
Cost per long call climbs: keep instructions stable and tune truncation retention

pitfalls.symptom: Calls drop at about the one hour mark
pitfalls.cause: The Azure realtime session maximum is 60 minutes
pitfalls.fix: Build reconnect logic that carries a state summary into the new session.

pitfalls.symptom: Cost per turn rises as a call goes on
pitfalls.cause: The whole conversation is resent each turn and mid-session edits bust the cache
pitfalls.fix: Keep instructions stable. `session.truncation.retention_ratio` defaults to 1.0, and 0.8 drops extra items so the cache stays valid longer [[r5]].

pitfalls.symptom: Old client code fails after migrating
pitfalls.cause: Beta header, endpoint and event names changed in GA
pitfalls.fix: Follow the beta-to-GA checklist, and on Azure send no `api-version`.

scenarios.title: Browser voice tutor
scenarios.situation: A web app lets students speak to a tutor. Thousands of students connect from home networks. Replies must feel immediate, and the API key must never reach the browser.
unknowns: Is a text transcript required for compliance?
scenarios.question: How do clients connect?

options.name: WebRTC with an ephemeral key minted by your server
options.why: WebRTC is the browser path with about 100 ms in Microsoft's table, and the short-lived key keeps your real key server-side [[r3]].
options.tradeoff: You build a small token endpoint and handle key expiry.

options.name: Browser WebSocket using a long-lived API key
options.why: It exposes a standing secret and is the slower transport.
options.tradeoff: A WebSocket is right for server-to-server links, never for shipping secrets to browsers.

options.name: Browser to your own WebSocket relay to the API
options.why: Keeps keys private and lets you log events.
options.tradeoff: Adds a hop and server load for every audio stream.

flips.if: Compliance needs every transcript stored before the model answers

flips.then: Use SIP or a telephony bridge.

scenarios.takeaway: Browsers get WebRTC and short-lived keys.

scenarios.title: Long advisory calls on Azure
scenarios.situation: Advisers hold 70 to 90 minute calls with customers through a voice agent on Azure OpenAI realtime. Calls must not drop, and context must survive.
unknowns: Can a short spoken pause be tolerated during reconnect?
scenarios.question: How do you handle the session limit?

options.name: Reconnect before the cap and carry a compact state summary into the new session
options.why: The 60-minute cap is documented [[r6]], so planned handover with a summary keeps context and stable instructions.
options.tradeoff: Needs a summariser and a brief spoken bridge.

options.name: Use truncation settings to extend the session
options.why: Truncation manages context length, not session lifetime.
options.tradeoff: Right for controlling cost and cache validity, not for beating the cap.

options.name: Hand every call to a human at 60 minutes
options.why: Simple and safe for sensitive advice.
options.tradeoff: Expensive in staff time and bad for customers mid-sentence.

flips.then: A simple reconnect for rare long calls is enough.
Re-check the limits on that platform before moving.

scenarios.takeaway: Treat the session cap as a design input, not an edge case.

quiz.q: In one turn the user speaks for 40 seconds and the assistant for 60 seconds. At 1 token per 100 ms of user audio and 1 per 50 ms of assistant audio, how many audio tokens is the turn?
quiz.explain: User: 40 s x 10 = 400 tokens. Assistant: 60 s x 20 = 1,200 tokens. Total 1,600.

quiz.q: A browser must open a realtime session. What is the safe way to authenticate?
options: Embed the API key in the page
Mint a short-lived ephemeral key on your server and give it to the browser
Ask users to paste their own key
Send audio to a public relay
quiz.explain: OpenAI mints ephemeral keys with `POST /v1/realtime/client_secrets` for client use. Embedding a standing key exposes it. User-pasted keys and public relays are unsafe or unmanaged.

quiz.q: Match each transport with its typical use.
quiz.explain: Microsoft lists about 100 ms for WebRTC, about 200 ms for WebSocket and varying latency for SIP.

flashcards.front: What latency does Microsoft list for realtime transports?
flashcards.back: About 100 ms for WebRTC (client apps), about 200 ms for WebSocket (server to server), and SIP varies (telephony).

flashcards.front: How are realtime audio tokens counted?
flashcards.back: 1 token per 100 ms of user audio and 1 per 50 ms of assistant audio. The whole conversation is resent each turn.

flashcards.front: What is the Azure realtime session cap?
flashcards.back: 60 minutes. Use the GA `/openai/v1` endpoint without `api-version`, and build reconnect logic.
